title: The PCOS Epidemic: A Crisis of Reproductive Health, Food Sovereignty, and Environmental Integrity
authors: Alka Singh, Parul Gupta, Satyendra Kumar Verma
affiliations: Affiliated to V. B. S. Purvanchal University, Jaunpur, Uttar Pradesh, India 222002

blocks.x: ABSTRACT:

Over the past century, Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) has moved far beyond its original classification as a purely reproductive disorder. It now stands as one of the most significant multi-system public-health challenges of our time. Current estimates indicate that the condition affects between 15 % and 20 % of women of reproductive age, and its prevalence continues to climb—especially in emerging economies—under the combined pressure of nutritional insecurity and progressive environmental deterioration. Key drivers include the widespread presence of endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) in ecosystems, the erosion of agricultural biodiversity, and the ongoing “nutrition transition” toward energy-dense, ultra-processed diets. In the present work we examine the epidemiological trajectory of PCOS, paying particular attention to the environmental and nutritional factors that accelerate its progression. We analyse how limited access to nutrient-dense, pesticide-free whole foods intensifies insulin resistance and hormonal imbalance. We further explore the concept of environmental security, demonstrating that chronic exposure to plastics, industrial pollutants and heavy metals functions as a potent catalyst for the PCOS phenotype. Keywords: PCOS complications; infertility; pregnancy loss; Type 2 diabetes; metabolic syndrome; cardiovascular disease; endocrine-disrupting chemicals; food sovereignty.
I. INTRODUCTION

Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is routinely labelled a contemporary “disorder,” yet its worldwide occurrence—ranging from 6 % to 20 % of women—reveals a far deeper biocultural problem. Restricting the condition to a failure of reproduction overlooks the larger evolutionary and environmental mismatch that underlies it [1,2]. PCOS is a multi-faceted state in which obesity, dyslipidaemia and elevated risk of Type 2 diabetes are not mere co-morbidities; they are the predictable consequences of a Palaeolithic physiology confronting a digital, hyper-caloric environment. By viewing PCOS through the lens of evolutionary mismatch, clinicians can shift from purely symptomatic treatment toward genuine metabolic restoration.
The Diagnostic Paradox

Although the medical community continues to rely on the Rotterdam criteria for diagnosis, this clinical snapshot frequently fails to capture the full complexity of the lived experience. The requirement of any two of three features—hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction (OD) and polycystic ovarian morphology (PCO) [3]—generates four distinct phenotypes that span a continuum of metabolic and reproductive states:
Phenotype A (Full Spectrum): Hyperandrogenism + OD + PCO
Phenotype B (Classic): Hyperandrogenism + OD
Phenotype C (Ovulatory): Hyperandrogenism + PCO
Phenotype D (Non-androgenic): OD + PCO [4].

PCOS is accompanied by a cluster of metabolic disturbances that include insulin resistance, obesity, dyslipidaemia and heightened long-term risk of Type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease (Figure 1) [5]. Insulin resistance (IR) constitutes one of the central pathophysiological features; it both intensifies the clinical presentation of PCOS and drives hyperandrogenism by elevating free androgen concentrations [6]. Excess androgens in turn amplify cutaneous and reproductive symptoms such as acne, hirsutism and anovulation [7]. The precise aetiology of PCOS remains incompletely understood, yet both intrinsic and extrinsic influences are known to be important. Genetic predisposition, epigenetic modification, dietary habits, lifestyle patterns and environmental exposures all contribute to disease onset and progression (Figure 1) [8,9]. When circulating insulin remains chronically elevated, the hormone ceases to act solely as a regulator of glucose and begins to function as a potent co-gonadotropin. This action stimulates ovarian theca cells to over-produce androgens, thereby establishing a self-reinforcing cycle of metabolic and reproductive disturbance: Metabolic Shift: Hyperinsulinaemia favours adipose storage and simultaneously dampens satiety signalling. Hormonal Cascades: Elevated insulin suppresses hepatic production of sex-hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), thereby increasing the free androgen fraction.
Physical Manifestation: Excess androgens interfere with the orderly process of follicular maturation and produce the external signs of the syndrome.
Gonadotropin Disruption: An altered ratio of luteinising hormone (LH) to follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) arrests normal follicular development [10].

The Insulin–Androgen Axis: Hyperinsulinaemia—arising when a thrifty metabolic genotype encounters refined carbohydrates—over-stimulates ovarian theca cells while concurrently lowering SHBG. The net result is a surge in bioactive testosterone [11,12].

The Silent Fire: Persistent metabolic stress ignites low-grade chronic inflammation. Immunological mediators recognised in PCOS pathogenesis include elevated interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumour-necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and C-reactive protein (CRP) [13–15] (Figure 1).

1. Environmental Realignment:

Because hyperinsulinaemia constitutes the principal driver of androgen excess, lifestyle modification is not merely an adjunct but the foundational clinical intervention. Prior to the introduction of exogenous hormones, the therapeutic objective is to lower systemic insulin through dietary change and physical activity, thereby attenuating ovarian testosterone production.
2. Managing Symptoms: The Pharmacological Toolkit

When lifestyle measures alone prove insufficient, a structured pharmacological sequence is employed. Interestingly, many of the “symptoms” that prompt women to seek medical attention once conferred selective advantages in ancestral environments.

blocks.x: Obesity aggravates virtually every clinical feature of PCOS; consequently, weight management is widely recommended as the initial therapeutic step. Lifestyle programmes typically combine dietary modification, increased physical activity and behavioural support aimed at sustainable weight reduction. Interestingly, women with and without PCOS report broadly similar dietary intakes and activity levels [15], implying that standard healthy-living principles remain applicable. Nevertheless, most lifestyle trials conducted in PCOS populations have been modest in size and the overall quality of evidence is low [16]. Meta-analyses of lifestyle interventions demonstrate favourable effects on body weight, free-androgen index and body-mass index (low-quality evidence). However, clear benefits for live-birth rates or restoration of regular menses have not been consistently shown. A randomised behavioural-modification trial published in 2019 reported a mean weight loss of approximately 2.1 % after four months, together with improved menstrual regularity, yet no significant change in ovulation frequency [17,18]. Participants who began the study with higher depressive scores were more likely to discontinue, underscoring the importance of integrated psychological support [19].

Exercise alone has been examined in several small studies employing heterogeneous protocols [20]. Evidence for an independent effect on reproductive or hormonal endpoints is limited, although moderate reductions in BMI are frequently observed. Long-term adherence to diet and activity recommendations remains challenging; real-world outcomes therefore tend to be less favourable than those recorded under trial conditions [21]. A focused analysis of four randomised lifestyle trials involving 221 women revealed an attrition rate of 47.1 %. Among those who remained, 63 % achieved at least 5 % weight loss. Women with better appointment attendance experienced both lower attrition and greater weight reduction. Multiple genetic, psychosocial, sociodemographic and physiological factors influence success [22,23]. Overall, the available data indicate that lifestyle intervention producing weight loss improves hyperandrogenism, metabolic parameters and quality of life, while evidence for reproductive benefit is still comparatively weak.

4. Treatment

Restoration of reproductive function in PCOS requires that the organism be persuaded it is no longer operating under chronic metabolic threat. According to current international guidelines, letrozole has become the preferred first-line agent for ovulation induction. By transiently lowering circulating oestrogen, the drug stimulates sufficient FSH release to overcome the “thrifty” follicular arrest and permit selection of a dominant follicle. Addition of metformin addresses the underlying insulin–androgen mismatch, thereby improving the intra-ovarian environment before induction is attempted.
Treatment Efficacy & Recommendation
Letrozole First-line choice. Superior to clomiphene citrate with respect to live-birth rate and shorter time-to-pregnancy.
Metformin Modest improvement in ovulation rates; most useful as a metabolic primer or in combination regimens.
Inositol High-quality evidence for improved live-birth rates in IVF settings remains limited; further data are required.
IVF protocols When advanced intervention is indicated, an antagonist protocol combined with a GnRH-agonist trigger is preferred to minimise the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).
III. EXPANDING THE HORIZON: WEIGHT AND METABOLIC HEALTH

As understanding of the PCOS “mismatch” deepens, the therapeutic armamentarium continues to expand: GLP-1 receptor agonists: These agents, originally developed for obesity and diabetes, demonstrate substantial promise and frequently outperform metformin with respect to weight reduction and metabolic stabilisation. Future directions: Ongoing research is evaluating combination regimens (metformin plus GLP-1 agonists) and exploring strategies to ensure equitable access for women in low-resource settings.

IV. CONCLUSION

The evolution of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome from a specialised reproductive diagnosis into a global multi-system public-health crisis highlights a profound biocultural mismatch. The rising prevalence of PCOS—now estimated at 6–20 % of women of reproductive age—cannot be explained solely by genetic predisposition; it is equally a product of nutritional insecurity and environmental degradation.
1. The Mechanistic Interplay

At the core of the syndrome lies hyperinsulinaemia, which functions as the primary engine of androgen excess. Chronic elevation of insulin acts as a co-gonadotropin, initiating a self-perpetuating cycle of metabolic and reproductive disturbance:

The Insulin–Androgen Axis: Hyperinsulinaemia over-stimulates ovarian theca cells and simultaneously suppresses SHBG, producing a surge in free, bioactive testosterone.
The “Silent Fire”: Metabolic friction generates low-grade chronic inflammation characterised by elevated IL-6, TNF-α and CRP.
2. Reframing Evolutionary “Assets”

A central argument of this work is that many PCOS-associated traits originated as adaptive Palaeolithic survival mechanisms that have become maladaptive in a modern, energy-abundant environment. Insulin resistance once conferred efficient energy storage during famine; hyperandrogenism once enhanced physical resilience. Recognition of this evolutionary history permits a shift from purely symptomatic suppression toward true metabolic reconciliation.
3. Clinical and Future Directives

Although pharmacological agents remain indispensable, lifestyle modification continues to be the primary means of lowering ovarian testosterone production. High attrition rates observed in lifestyle programmes (approximately 47 % in some trials) underline the necessity of integrated behavioural support. Looking ahead, management of PCOS should prioritise:
Fertility: Adoption of letrozole as first-line therapy because of superior live-birth rates relative to clomiphene citrate.
Metabolic innovation: Wider use of GLP-1 receptor agonists, which often surpass traditional therapies in weight reduction and metabolic control.
Environmental integrity: Systematic reduction of exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals and reversal of the nutrition transition that currently catalyses the PCOS phenotype
